description: NHI risk rules. Declarative only: the scoring engine (not yet written) reads this file plus an inventory JSON. Points come from scoring.tierPoints via each rule's severity; rules never carry their own numbers, so there is one place to change a weight.

evaluation.clockNote: Rules never read the wall clock. 'expired' means endDateTime <= scanStartUtc; 'active' means endDateTime > scanStartUtc.
evaluation.inputs: Inventory JSON only. No Graph calls in Phase 3.
evaluation.granularity: At most one finding per rule per identity (appId). The finding's evidence lists every matching item. NHI-004 fires once at the HIGHEST matching tier, so an app with five High permissions scores 25, not 125.

credentialSources.note: Both objects must always be read. seed-11 keeps its only credential on the service principal (regression test).

ownerTypes.source: identities[].ownerType, assigned by the Phase 2 scanner (ManagedIdentity is decided first, then appOwnerOrganizationId against this tenant and the Microsoft tenants).
ownerTypes.policy: Every rule covers every type unless its appliesToReason states why not. Unknown is never excluded ('never guess'). Only NHI-001 excludes anything (Microsoft, ManagedIdentity).

resourceResolution.method: Build an index of identities[].servicePrincipal.id -> identities[].appId from the inventory. For each appRoleAssignments[] / oauth2PermissionGrants[] entry, look up resourceId in that index and compare the resolved appId. resourceDisplayName is a label only and is never used to decide a match.
resourceResolution.why: resourceId is a tenant-local service principal object id, and a display name can be chosen by anyone; the appId of Microsoft Graph is fixed and cannot be reused by a tenant app.
resourceResolution.unresolved: If a resourceId is not in the index, the entry cannot match any rule. The engine must record it as a scan warning (unresolvedResource), not fail silently. Currently 0 of 6 references are unresolved in the newest inventory.

evaluation.lifetimeDays: floor((endDateTime - startDateTime).TotalDays). Whole days absorb the client-side end vs server-side start skew noted in TODO.md; NHI-002 fires when lifetimeDays > 180, so exactly 180 does not fire.

scoring.scoreCapNote: DECIDED: no cap. Scores rank identities and a cap would flatten the top of the ranking. Theoretical max is 131 (001:10 + 002:10 + 003:3 + 004:40 + 005:40 + 007:10 + 008:3 = 116, plus the 15-point uplift), so scores are not a 0-100 scale.
scoring.singleFindingRule: An identity with exactly one finding scores exactly tierPoints[severity]. Combination uplifts can never fire on a single finding (seed-11 constraint).

rules.name: No owner / sponsor
rules.appliesToReason: Excludes Microsoft first-party (never owned by tenant users; ~78 meaningless findings) and ManagedIdentity (no owner concept; its lifecycle follows the Azure resource it is attached to). ThirdParty is included on purpose: ownerless consented SaaS apps are a real AC-2 gap, and will be noisy. Unknown is never excluded.
rules.logic: application.owners and servicePrincipal.owners are both empty (or absent).
rules.rationale: Nobody is accountable for the identity: no one to ask what it is for, rotate its credentials, or approve its removal. This is a governance gap, not by itself exploitable.
rules.remediation: Assign at least one owner (two preferred) or a sponsor.

rules.name: Client secret lifetime over 180 days
rules.appliesToReason: All types: any service principal in this tenant can carry a secret that someone here created, whoever published the app, including hidden credentials added to third-party or Microsoft service principals.
rules.logic: Any client secret (passwordCredentials, on application OR servicePrincipal) with lifetimeDays > 180. Evaluated whether or not the secret has expired.
rules.rationale: Long-lived secrets widen the window in which a leaked secret is useful. Fires on expired secrets too, because the question is how the credential was issued. It does NOT mean the secret is still usable; that is NHI-007.
rules.thresholdNote: 180 days is a project threshold. Microsoft recommends under 12 months for secrets (max 24); 180 days is Microsoft's recommended maximum for certificates. See risk-model.md.
rules.remediation: Shorten lifetime, or better, replace with workload identity federation / managed identity.

rules.name: Expired credential still attached
rules.appliesToReason: All types: stale credentials on any service principal in this tenant are this tenant's cleanup responsibility.
rules.logic: Any credential (secret or certificate, on application OR servicePrincipal) with endDateTime <= scanStartUtc.
rules.rationale: Dead credentials are clutter that hides live ones and signals nobody is cleaning up. Not exploitable on its own.

rules.name: High-risk application permission granted
rules.severityNote: Severity = highest tier among matching granted permissions.
rules.appliesToReason: All types: application permission grants are decided by this tenant whoever published the app. Third-party consent and managed-identity privilege are exactly what this rule must catch; Microsoft first-party stays in scope because a tenant admin can still add risky grants to it.
rules.logic: servicePrincipal.appRoleAssignments[] where the entry's resourceId resolves (see evaluation.resourceResolution) to a service principal whose appId == resourceAppId, and permission is in a tier below. GRANTED application permissions only: requested-but-not-consented (seed-07) and delegated-only (seed-08) do not count.

tiers.meaning: Privilege-granting: the holder can grant itself or others more privilege, so the practical ceiling is Global Administrator.
Broad data or directory access, but no verified direct path to grant privilege.

reviewNotes.Directory.ReadWrite.All: Kept in High. Third-party testing (SpecterOps, 2024) found it cannot add credentials, grant app roles, promote to Global Admin or change role-assignable groups. See risk-model.md for the evidence and caveats.

rules.tierListNote: The High list is the NHI-008 list minus the Critical entries. UNRESEARCHED, PROJECT CONVENTION: it has not been checked against external sources. Research is a TODO.md item; see risk-model.md.
rules.rationale: Application permissions work without a signed-in user and are tenant-wide, so impact is what the permission lets the identity do across the whole tenant.
rules.remediation: Remove the permission, or replace it with a narrower one (resource-specific consent, *.OwnedBy variants).

rules.name: Privileged directory role assigned to a service principal
rules.appliesToReason: All types: directory role assignments are tenant-controlled whatever the identity type; managed identities and third-party apps holding privileged roles are in scope on purpose.
rules.logic: servicePrincipal.directoryRoles[] where assignmentType is in assignmentTypes and roleDefinitionId is in privilegedRoles[].roleDefinitionId.
rules.assignmentTypesNote: Eligible (PIM) assignments are recorded by the inventory but do not fire. See risk-model.md and the TODO.md item on service principal self-activation.
rules.privilegedRolesNote: Static list of built-in role template IDs. Matching is by roleDefinitionId only; label is for humans (a custom role can copy a display name but not a built-in template ID). Each role is marked 'This is a privileged role' on Microsoft's permissions-reference page, which the privileged-roles-permissions page points to for the list. Microsoft's own isPrivileged flag is not in the inventory and Phase 3 may not call Graph, so this list must be maintained by hand. It is a deliberate subset, not every role Microsoft marks privileged.
rules.rationale: A standing privileged directory role gives the identity tenant-wide control; for Application Administrator that includes managing credentials on apps.
rules.remediation: Remove the role assignment; use a least-privilege custom role or Graph permission instead.

rules.name: No sign-in in 90+ days
rules.appliesToReason: All types (draft): an unused service principal is an AC-2 gap whoever published it. Deferred, so currently inert.
rules.deferredReason: Sign-in activity cannot be seeded; every seed shows signInActivity = null. How 'never signed in' is treated is undecided. The engine must skip deferred rules, so they add 0 to every score.
rules.logic: (draft) servicePrincipal.signInActivity.lastSignInDateTime older than 90 days before scanStartUtc. Null handling TBD.

rules.name: Active client secret in use
rules.appliesToReason: All types: a live secret on any service principal in this tenant is a usable credential, including hidden credentials on third-party or Microsoft service principals.
rules.logic: Any client secret (passwordCredentials, on application OR servicePrincipal) with endDateTime > scanStartUtc. Certificates do not count.
rules.rationale: A usable shared secret can be copied, leaked and replayed. Microsoft says client secrets should not be used in production. This is the 'armed' half of the combination uplift.
rules.remediation: Replace with workload identity federation (OIDC) or a managed identity, then delete the secret.

rules.name: Tenant-wide consent to a high-risk delegated permission
rules.appliesToReason: All types: tenant-wide consent is a tenant decision for any app, and third-party apps are the main target. Microsoft first-party stays in scope (for example Microsoft Graph Command Line Tools holds AllPrincipals grants today).
rules.logic: servicePrincipal.oauth2PermissionGrants[] where consentType == 'AllPrincipals', the entry's resourceId resolves (see evaluation.resourceResolution) to a service principal whose appId == resourceAppId, and any entry of scopes[] is in the list below.
rules.rationale: Delegated permissions are limited by the signed-in user's own rights, so impact is lower than the same application permission. Low but non-zero.
rules.remediation: Revoke the tenant-wide grant; require per-user consent or narrower scopes.

combinations.name: Armed privilege
combinations.rationale: Privilege is only dangerous to the extent someone can authenticate as the identity. An active client secret is a usable credential. NHI-002 is deliberately NOT in the condition: it can fire on an expired secret, which proves nothing about current usability.

consideredAndRejected.name: Unattended privilege
consideredAndRejected.rejectedBecause: Ownerless is a governance gap, not exploitability. It does not make the identity easier to abuse, so it should not raise the risk score of the privilege.

ms-privileged-roles.title: Privileged roles and permissions in Microsoft Entra ID
ms-privileged-roles.verifiedFor: Defines the PRIVILEGED label (itself in preview); its example output shows Application Administrator with IsPrivileged = True. It does NOT list the roles itself; it points to the permissions-reference page for the list.

ms-permissions-reference.title: Microsoft Entra built-in roles
ms-permissions-reference.verifiedFor: Template IDs for the five NHI-005 roles, and the sentence 'This is a privileged role' in each role's section (read directly for Global Administrator, Privileged Role Administrator, Privileged Authentication Administrator, Application Administrator, Cloud Application Administrator).

ms-graph-permissions.title: Microsoft Graph permissions reference
ms-graph-permissions.verifiedFor: Official caution text on Application.ReadWrite.All (credential management lets an app act as other entities) and AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All (lets an app grant additional privileges to itself, other applications or any user).

ms-add-credentials.title: Add and manage app credentials in Microsoft Entra ID
ms-add-credentials.verifiedFor: Client secrets 'should not be used in production'; lifetime capped at 24 months; Microsoft recommends under 12 months; federated credentials recommended for workloads such as GitHub Actions.

ms-enforce-secret-standards.title: Tutorial: Enforce secret and certificate standards using application management policies
ms-enforce-secret-standards.verifiedFor: Recommends disabling client secrets; 180 days is the recommended maximum for CERTIFICATES (not secrets).

ms-migrate-from-secrets.title: Migrate applications away from secret-based authentication
ms-migrate-from-secrets.verifiedFor: Exposed secrets let an attacker escalate depending on the app's permissions; recommends managed identities and federated identity.

bloodhound-grant-app-roles.title: BloodHound edge: AZMGGrantAppRoles
bloodhound-grant-app-roles.verifiedFor: Third-party: AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All can grant RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory to a service principal you control, which can then assign Global Administrator.

specterops-dirrw.title: Directory.ReadWrite.All Is Not As Powerful As You Might Think
specterops-dirrw.verifiedFor: Third-party testing, 2024: see risk-model.md. Not Microsoft guidance; Graph behaviour can change.

nist-800-53.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 (Update 1)
nist-800-53.verifiedFor: Publication page exists and is Rev. 5. AC-2, AC-6 and IA-5 mappings come from CLAUDE.md; control text not re-read here.
